content.title: About
content.content: Turkey (Meleagris gallopavo) is a domesticated bird raised for its tender white meat. The skin is often left on because it contains beneficial fats and becomes crispy when cooked properly. The meat is high in protein, low in calories, and provides B‑vitamins, iron, and zinc.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkey is the centerpiece of Thanksgiving meals in the United States.
White turkey meat contains less fat than dark meat, while the skin retains some healthy monounsaturated fats.
In the wild, turkeys can fly short distances, but domestic breeds are largely flightless.
Turkey meat is popular in diet plans due to its low calorie density.
When roasted, turkey skin forms a flavorful crust that locks in juices.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: White turkey meat provides about 23 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: The lean meat contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey supplies niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals: iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals are important for blood formation and immune function.

items.title: Beneficial fats in the skin
items.content: The skin contains monounsaturated fatty acids that can help maintain healthy cholesterol levels.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey meat or skin.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked turkey can harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: High sodium in processed products
items.content: Smoked or cured turkey often contains added salt, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Overeating the skin
items.content: While the skin provides healthy fats, excessive consumption adds extra calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Turkey can be roasted, boiled, grilled, or steamed. For a crispy texture, cook the skin until golden brown. The meat is versatile in salads, sandwiches, soups, and stews. To reduce calories, remove the skin before cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh turkey refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for 2‑3 days. Freeze raw or cooked turkey at ‑18 °C for up to 12 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor, slimy texture, or discoloration.
